h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in Des Moines
intro: Des Moines has grown steadily for years on the strength of insurance, finance, government and health care employers, and its housing market has followed. Demand reaches well beyond the western suburbs. Investors are active in the city's older neighborhoods, from the brick Tudors and colonials of Beaverdale to the foursquares and bungalows of Highland Park and Oak Park, the student rentals around Drake University and the modest frame houses on the south side. Most of that stock is old enough to need real systems work, a share of it sits in river-adjacent areas that have flooded before, and every rental in the city falls under local inspection rules. Genstone Construction manages renovations for investors, lenders and servicers in Des Moines and the surrounding Polk County communities. Vetted, licensed local contractors perform the work, and our estimators and field managers direct it from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters. A free Pre-Offer Rehab Review comes first, then an itemized scope, a draw schedule that follows completed work and one field manager from start to finish, with no upfront payment.
housingStock:
Des Moines' older neighborhoods were built in recognizable bands, and each band carries a different rehab profile.

The oldest surviving homes sit near downtown. Sherman Hill, a historic district just northwest of the core, is known for its Victorian and Queen Anne houses, many of which were divided into apartments and later restored. Capitol Park and the streets east of the Capitol hold older frame homes of similar age, often more modest.

The north side, including Highland Park, Oak Park, River Bend and Union Park, grew in the early twentieth century with foursquares, Craftsman bungalows and simple two-story frame houses. Many have stone or brick foundations, balloon framing, plaster walls and upgrades of varying quality layered over the decades. The Drake neighborhood around Drake University shares that era and style, with a large share of houses operated as student rentals.

Beaverdale, northwest of downtown, is famous for its brick homes from the 1920s through the 1940s, often called Beaverdale bricks: one-and-a-half and two-story Tudor Revival and Colonial Revival houses with solid masonry walls, arched doorways and steep roofs. They are well built but come with their own needs, including tuckpointing, original steel or wood windows, plaster repair and aging boilers.

On the south side, Indianola Hills and South Park mix early twentieth century frame homes with post-war ranches and Cape Cods. The east side and the city's outer edges are dominated by post-war ranches and split-levels, while Waterbury and the far west side include larger homes from the early and middle twentieth century.

Across these bands, the typical rehab includes lead-safe work, electrical upgrades, replacement of galvanized and cast-iron plumbing, foundation moisture control and radon testing, which matters in Iowa more than in most states.

commonIssues.title: Radon in Iowa basements
commonIssues.body: Iowa is widely recognized as having some of the highest radon levels in the country, and basements across Des Moines are no exception. Any rehab that adds bedrooms or living space to a lower level, or that sells or rents to families, should include radon testing and mitigation where results call for it. A sub-slab mitigation system is a modest line item compared with the value of a finished basement, and buyers increasingly ask about it.

commonIssues.title: River and flash flood exposure
commonIssues.body: The Des Moines and Raccoon rivers have flooded the city before, including major events in 1993 and 2008, and low-lying areas near the rivers and creeks remain vulnerable. Even outside mapped floodplains, intense summer storms can overwhelm drainage and push water into basements. Checking flood zone status, past insurance claims and signs of prior water in the basement is essential before buying, and it shapes how much finished space makes sense.

commonIssues.title: Masonry on Beaverdale brick homes
commonIssues.body: The solid brick walls that make Beaverdale homes appealing also need care. Mortar joints erode after decades of freeze-thaw cycles, chimneys lose their crowns, and window sills and lintels can crack or rust. Repointing with the wrong mortar can damage older brick. A realistic scope prices tuckpointing, chimney repair and window work separately, since these items often surprise investors who budget only for interior updates.

commonIssues.title: Systems in north side foursquares
commonIssues.body: Early twentieth century homes in Highland Park, Oak Park, River Bend and the Drake area often still have knob-and-tube wiring hidden in plaster walls, galvanized water lines, cast-iron drains and old boilers or converted gravity furnaces. Lenders and insurers may balk at remaining knob-and-tube. These systems are frequently the largest part of the budget, and pricing them during a Pre-Offer Rehab Review keeps them out of change orders.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint and student-rental wear
commonIssues.body: Most of the city's older housing predates 1978, so lead-safe practices apply to the majority of renovations that disturb paint. Houses near Drake University face an additional challenge: years of student tenancy often leave damaged doors and trim, worn floors, makeshift bedrooms and amateur repairs. A durable renovation with verified egress from every bedroom brings these properties back to a sound, rentable standard.

investorMarket:
Investment strategies in Des Moines follow the city's neighborhood patterns fairly closely.

Buy-and-hold and BRRRR investors concentrate on the north side, in Highland Park, Oak Park, River Bend and Union Park, and on the south side, where older single-family homes and duplexes can be purchased at prices that leave room for a full rehab. Tenant demand comes from the city's large workforce in insurance, finance, health care, logistics and government. Rehabs in these areas focus on systems, safety and durable finishes rather than design.

Flippers are most active in Beaverdale, the Drake area, Waterbury and parts of the south side near Gray's Lake, where owner-occupant buyers compete for updated older homes with character. Beaverdale brick houses in particular draw strong buyer interest, and a careful update that respects their architecture tends to sell well. Post-war ranches on the east side and the city's edges also make solid flips for first-time buyers.

Student rentals around Drake University are a distinct niche, with demand tied to the academic calendar and a heavy emphasis on durability and bedroom count.

Small multifamily appears as older converted houses in Sherman Hill and near downtown, up-and-down and side-by-side duplexes on the north and south sides, and 1960s and 1970s fourplexes scattered throughout the city.

The western and northern suburbs, including West Des Moines, Urbandale, Clive, Johnston and Ankeny, offer newer housing with higher prices and lighter rehab scopes, where flips compete with new construction.
permits:
Building permits in Des Moines are handled through the city's Permit and Development Center, which reviews plans and schedules inspections for structural, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work. Remodels that move walls, replace roofs, finish basements, add bathrooms, enlarge windows for egress or alter mechanical systems generally require permits. In Iowa, contractors must be registered with the state, and electricians, plumbers and mechanical contractors are licensed at the state level.

Rental property is a key consideration in Des Moines. Iowa law requires larger cities to maintain housing codes with rental inspection programs, and Des Moines requires rental properties to be registered and inspected under its housing code. A renovation intended for rent should be scoped to pass that inspection, with attention to smoke and carbon monoxide detection, egress, electrical safety, handrails and working heat.

Properties in floodplain areas can be subject to additional requirements, especially for substantial improvements, and Sherman Hill is a local historic district where exterior changes may require review. Suburbs such as West Des Moines, Urbandale, Ankeny and Johnston each run their own building and rental programs. Genstone confirms the jurisdiction and any special requirements during scoping and builds the permit and inspection steps into the schedule.
climate:
Des Moines has a classic continental climate with cold, snowy winters and hot, humid summers, and both seasons affect renovation work. Winter freeze-thaw cycles crack masonry, heave steps and walks and push on foundation walls, while ice dams form on poorly insulated older homes. Vacant houses can freeze if heat is lost, so winter acquisitions should be checked for burst pipes before scoping.

Spring and summer bring heavy thunderstorms, hail, high winds and occasionally tornadoes, along with intense rain that can flood basements and low-lying streets. Roofs, siding and gutters take the brunt of storm damage.

For scheduling, roofing, masonry, concrete, siding and exterior painting fit best from spring through fall, with an eye on summer storm season. Interior renovations continue year-round in a heated house. Student rentals near Drake follow the academic calendar, with summer the main renovation window.

faqs.q: Do Des Moines rentals have to be inspected?
faqs.a: Yes. Des Moines requires rental properties to be registered and inspected under its housing code, in line with Iowa law that requires larger cities to maintain rental inspection programs. We scope rental renovations to meet common inspection items, including smoke and carbon monoxide detection, egress from sleeping rooms, safe electrical, handrails and working heat, so the property is ready when the inspector arrives. Suburbs have their own programs.

faqs.q: Should I worry about radon in a Des Moines rehab?
faqs.a: It deserves attention. Iowa has some of the highest radon levels in the country, and basements are where it collects. If you plan to finish a lower level, rent to families or sell to owner-occupants, testing is wise, and mitigation is a relatively modest cost when results are high. We include radon testing and mitigation as a clear line item so it is part of the plan from the start.

faqs.q: Is a Beaverdale brick home a good flip?
faqs.a: It can be. Beaverdale brick houses draw strong buyer interest, and a well-executed update that respects their Tudor and colonial character tends to perform well. The risks are in masonry, windows, plumbing, electrical and heating, which can be costly on homes of that age. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices those items alongside the finish plan so you know whether the numbers work before you buy.

faqs.q: Where is Genstone's office for Des Moines projects?
faqs.a: Genstone's only office is in Romeoville, Illinois, and that is where our estimators, field managers and billing team work on Des Moines renovations. Vetted, licensed and insured contractors in central Iowa handle the construction. Your field manager shares photos, milestones and documentation throughout the project, so you can track progress closely without making trips to the property, which matters for investors who live outside Iowa.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Des Moines, IA | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Des Moines fix and flip renovations for Beaverdale brick homes, Drake-area houses and east side ranches, priced against local comps with work-based draws.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Des Moines
fix-flip.intro: Buyers shopping for an updated older home in Des Moines tend to know what they want. In Beaverdale, they are looking for a brick Tudor or colonial with its arches, trim and hardwood intact and a kitchen that finally works. Near Drake and in Waterbury, they want character combined with modern systems. On the east side, first-time buyers want an updated ranch with a newer furnace and a dry basement at a sensible price. A Des Moines flip succeeds when the scope matches those expectations and handles the hidden work that inspectors will find. Genstone Construction plans flips around that reality. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs, refines your after-repair value against recent nearby sales and tells you plainly whether the deal supports your offer, followed by an itemized scope with finish options and a field manager who directs the job to listing.

sections.body: Beaverdale brick homes are among the most recognizable houses in Des Moines, and they draw buyers who appreciate their solid construction and period details. A successful flip respects that character while modernizing what buyers cannot see. That usually means refinishing hardwood floors, preserving arched doorways and original trim where possible, and designing a kitchen that fits the house rather than fighting it. Behind the walls, the work often includes replacing knob-and-tube or outdated wiring, swapping galvanized supply lines for modern piping, updating or replacing older boilers, and addressing basement moisture. On the exterior, tuckpointing, chimney repairs and window restoration or replacement can be significant line items, and they need to be done with mortar and materials compatible with the original brick. Our estimators price each of these items separately and match finishes to recent Beaverdale sales, so you can see exactly where the money goes and avoid overbuilding a house on a street where the top sale was a modest, well-done update.

sections.h2: Ranches, Cape Cods and first-time buyers
sections.body: Post-war ranches and Cape Cods on the east side, the south side and the city's outer edges make up a large share of Des Moines flips. Their buyers are often first-time owners using FHA or conventional loans, and they focus on practical value: an updated kitchen and bath, new flooring, fresh paint, a furnace and water heater with years of life left, a roof without storm damage and a basement that stays dry. Open main floors are popular where structure allows. These houses may contain asbestos in floor tile, mastic or duct wrap, which must be tested and handled properly if a remodel disturbs it. Radon testing is wise, especially if the basement will be marketed as usable space. Because buyers in these neighborhoods compare your listing with similarly priced updated homes, we keep finishes in line with comps and put the budget into the items appraisers and inspectors notice most. That discipline keeps your margin intact and helps the house pass FHA or conventional appraisal without repair conditions.

Des Moines buyers almost always order inspections, and older homes tend to generate predictable findings: outdated wiring, galvanized plumbing, aging heating equipment, wet basements, storm-damaged roofs and missing handrails. Addressing these items under permits from the city's Permit and Development Center, and documenting the work with photos, gives buyers and lenders confidence and limits renegotiation. Timing matters too. Roofing, masonry, siding and concrete should be completed in warmer months, ideally before the heavy storm season peaks, or planned carefully if the house is bought in late fall. Interior work proceeds through winter as long as the house is heated. Many investors aim to finish interior renovations during the cold months and list in spring, when buyer activity typically increases. Our draw schedule separates exterior and interior phases, so weather only delays the work it affects, and your field manager reports progress and flags problems such as hidden water damage early enough to adjust your plan.

faqs.q: How much should I spend on finishes in a Des Moines flip?
faqs.a: It depends on the neighborhood. Beaverdale and Waterbury buyers often reward quality finishes and preserved character, while east side ranch buyers focus on clean, durable updates and reliable systems. Our estimates can show more than one finish plan with costs, letting you compare the investment against recent sales instead of guessing what buyers will pay. The decision is made before purchase, not halfway through the job.

faqs.q: Can you handle masonry work on a brick flip?
faqs.a: Yes. We scope tuckpointing, chimney repairs, sill and lintel replacement and other masonry work with materials compatible with older brick. Using the wrong mortar can damage historic masonry, so we specify appropriate products. Exterior masonry is best done in warmer months, and we schedule it accordingly within the project plan. Buyers of Beaverdale homes often look closely at chimneys and mortar, so documented masonry work helps at inspection.

faqs.q: What does a Des Moines flip cost me before work starts?
faqs.a: Nothing. Genstone takes no upfront payment on flips. Draws are released for stages of work your field manager has completed and documented, and the final payment follows completion and your approval. Dumpster and debris removal are already priced into the estimate, which is helpful on older homes where plaster and basement cleanouts generate a lot of material in the first days.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Des Moines, IA | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR renovations in Des Moines for north side and south side homes, scoped to the refinance appraisal, rental inspections and Iowa storms and radon.
brrrr.intro: Des Moines has the ingredients BRRRR investors look for: older houses on the north and south sides that can still be bought below renovated comps, a large and steady workforce that rents, and enough recent sales of updated homes to support a refinance appraisal. The catch is that the city's rental inspection program, Iowa's radon levels and the region's storms all shape what a sound rehab has to include. A BRRRR property here needs to appraise well, pass the rental inspection and stand up to years of tenants and weather. Genstone Construction scopes Des Moines BRRRR projects with all three in mind. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work and checks the after-repair value before you commit capital, and our draw schedule follows completed work the way rehab lenders expect. Genstone Financial also writes DSCR rental loans if you want the refinance handled within the Genstone Companies.

sections.h2: Finding the BRRRR spread in Des Moines
sections.body: In Des Moines, the strongest BRRRR candidates tend to be houses that look dated but are structurally sound. Foursquares and bungalows in Highland Park, Oak Park and Union Park often sell below updated comps because of original kitchens, old wiring and tired mechanicals, while their framing and foundations remain serviceable. South side frame homes and post-war ranches in Indianola Hills and South Park can follow the same pattern. Properties with serious foundation movement, major flood history or extensive fire damage can still work, but the cost of correcting those problems rarely shows up in the appraisal, so the purchase price has to reflect it. Before you buy, we also check whether the property sits in a mapped floodplain, since that affects insurance, renovation requirements and resale. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review weighs these factors and gives you a realistic cost and value range, so you can bid confidently on the right houses and pass on the ones that only work under optimistic assumptions.

sections.h2: Renovating for the appraisal and the rental inspection
sections.body: Appraisers in Des Moines compare your property with recent sales of updated homes nearby, so the renovation should place it clearly in that group. That generally means an updated kitchen with durable cabinets and counters, a renovated bath, refinished or new flooring, fresh paint and lighting, and documented upgrades to heating, electrical and plumbing. A dry basement and a roof free of storm damage support the valuation. At the same time, the property must pass the city's rental inspection, which focuses on life safety: smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, egress from sleeping rooms, safe electrical, handrails and guards, working heat and sound plumbing. We combine both sets of requirements into one scope so the house can be appraised, inspected and leased without repeat work. Permits are pulled through the Permit and Development Center, and your field manager keeps a photo record and documentation package that supports the refinance lender's review and the inspector's visit.

sections.h2: Built to last through Iowa weather
sections.body: A BRRRR property is meant to be held, and in Des Moines durability means planning for cold winters, summer storms and radon. Roofs, gutters and siding should be in good condition after the rehab, since hail and wind damage are common and repairs are disruptive with tenants in place. Basements need reliable water control: grading, downspout extensions, sealed cracks and, where water enters, drain tile and a sump pump with a dependable discharge. Radon testing and mitigation protect tenants who use the lower level for laundry, storage or living space. Inside, luxury vinyl plank or tile at entries and in kitchens and baths handles snow, salt and spills. A newer furnace and water heater reduce midwinter breakdowns, and attic insulation lowers heating costs for tenants. Simple, standard fixtures keep repairs quick. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the work our crews install, while tenant damage and ordinary wear are excluded, which makes durable material choices the best long-term protection.

faqs.q: Which Des Moines neighborhoods work for BRRRR?
faqs.a: Many investors focus on the north side, including Highland Park, Oak Park and Union Park, and on south side areas such as Indianola Hills and South Park. These neighborhoods offer older homes that can be bought below renovated comps and steady rental demand. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review compares repair costs and after-repair values for specific properties so you can decide with real numbers.

faqs.q: Will a BRRRR rehab pass the Des Moines rental inspection?
faqs.a: We scope projects around the items rental inspections commonly check, such as detectors, egress, electrical safety, handrails and working heat. The inspection itself is performed by the city, so we cannot control its result, but building those requirements into the renovation reduces the chance of corrections. If additional items are noted, your field manager coordinates repairs and the reinspection quickly so leasing is not delayed.

faqs.q: Do flood zones matter for a BRRRR deal?
faqs.a: They can matter a great deal. Properties in mapped floodplains may require flood insurance, which affects cash flow, and substantial improvements can trigger additional requirements. Basement finishing may be limited. We check flood zone status during scoping and adjust the plan, but you should also confirm insurance costs and lender requirements before buying. River Bend and other low-lying areas deserve particular care.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Des Moines, IA | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Des Moines rental renovations for single-family homes, duplexes and Drake student rentals, built to the city's rental inspection and Iowa weather.
rental-renovation.h1: Rental Property Renovations in Des Moines
rental-renovation.intro: Rental owners in Des Moines manage a mix of property types: north side foursquares leased to working families, south side ranches, duplexes across older neighborhoods and student houses around Drake University. All of them fall under the city's rental registration and inspection requirements, and all of them face Iowa's cold winters, summer storms and high radon levels. The renovations that pay off are the ones that pass inspection on the first visit, keep basements dry, hold up to tenant turnover and reduce emergency calls. Genstone Construction renovates Des Moines rentals to a consistent, inspection-ready standard. We write a portfolio specification for finishes and systems, plan work around vacancies, seasons and the academic calendar, and assign a field manager who coordinates vetted local contractors and keeps documentation visible. After the rehab, sister companies Genstone Property Management and Genstone Field Services can take over leasing support, make-readies and upkeep if you want them to.

sections.body: Des Moines rental inspections focus on health and safety, so a rental renovation should meet those standards from the start. That means properly placed smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, egress windows in every sleeping room, safe electrical without exposed wiring or overloaded circuits, sturdy handrails and guards, working heat and hot water, and plumbing free of leaks. In the city's older homes, meeting these standards often requires replacing remaining knob-and-tube wiring, upgrading panels, enlarging basement bedroom windows, repairing stairways and porches and replacing galvanized supply lines. We put these requirements into a portfolio specification so every property you own reaches the same baseline. Finishes follow the same approach: durable flooring, a consistent paint palette, standard fixtures and cabinets that hold up to heavy use. That consistency makes inspections more predictable, speeds up turns, and lets your property manager stock the same parts for every unit across the portfolio, which simplifies maintenance and lowers costs over a long hold period.

Houses near Drake University serve a tenant base that turns over regularly and uses properties hard. Renovations there focus on durability and safety. Every bedroom needs legal egress and smoke detection, and the bedroom count must match what the property can legally support. Flooring should be water-resistant and easy to repair, doors and hardware should be sturdy, and kitchens and baths should use simple, durable fixtures. Electrical systems often need upgrading to handle multiple occupants with modern devices. Many of these homes are early twentieth century houses with plaster, older wiring and aging plumbing, so systems work frequently accompanies the cosmetic refresh. Timing follows the academic year. Summer is the main window for larger renovations, and the weeks before fall move-in are crowded. We recommend scoping in spring, ordering materials early and starting work as soon as tenants leave. Your field manager tracks each property against its move-in date and flags any risk early, so units are ready when students arrive.

The costliest rental problems in Des Moines usually involve water and weather. Summer storms can overwhelm gutters and push water into basements, hail and wind damage roofs and siding, and winter cold can freeze pipes in poorly insulated walls. Renovation is the time to address these risks. We look at grading, gutters, downspouts, foundation cracks and sump pumps when basements take on water, replace aging furnaces and water heaters before they fail, and insulate or reroute vulnerable plumbing. Radon testing and mitigation protect tenants who use lower levels. Between full renovations, Genstone Field Services can handle make-ready work, inspections, occupied maintenance and code compliance, so the property stays with the same group that renovated it. When a turn reveals a larger issue, your field manager can scope it as a separate project with its own draw schedule. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the work Genstone performs, though tenant damage and ordinary wear are outside it.

faqs.q: Can Genstone renovate Des Moines rentals with tenants in place?
faqs.a: For many projects, yes. Furnace and water heater replacement, electrical updates, radon mitigation and exterior work can often be completed while tenants live in the home, with access scheduled in advance. Larger interior renovations usually work best during a vacancy. Your field manager coordinates with you or your property manager and keeps work areas safe, using lead-safe containment where older paint is disturbed.

faqs.q: How do you prepare student rentals for fall move-in?
faqs.a: We recommend scoping units in spring, finalizing materials early and starting work as soon as tenants move out. Larger tasks are completed first, followed by paint, cleaning and final details. Your field manager tracks every property against its move-in date and reports progress, so you know well ahead of time whether each unit will be ready for the students arriving in August.

faqs.q: Do you manage renovations across a rental portfolio?
faqs.a: Yes. We work with individual investors, funds and institutional owners, and our network of licensed local contractors allows us to handle multiple Des Moines properties at the same time. Each property has its own scope, estimate and draw schedule, while a shared specification keeps materials and finishes consistent, making future maintenance and turns more efficient. You can follow every property's progress from one place.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & 2–4 Unit Renovation in Des Moines, IA | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Des Moines duplex and 2–4 unit renovations: Sherman Hill conversions, north side duplexes and 1960s–70s fourplexes, phased around tenants and inspections.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovations in Des Moines
multifamily-renovation.intro: Small multifamily property in Des Moines takes several forms. In Sherman Hill and the older neighborhoods near downtown, large Victorian and early twentieth century houses were divided into apartments decades ago. On the north and south sides, up-and-down and side-by-side duplexes sit among single-family homes, and 1960s and 1970s fourplexes appear throughout the city, often with shared laundry and a central stair. Each type has different renovation needs, but all share the challenges of shared systems, fire separation, rental inspections and tenants who may still be in place. Genstone Construction renovates Des Moines duplexes and 2–4 unit buildings for investors, phasing work around occupied units, pricing shared systems separately and planning for inspection requirements. Every project begins with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review and an itemized scope, and one field manager oversees the entire building.

sections.h2: Converted houses in Sherman Hill and near downtown
sections.body: Many of the older houses in Sherman Hill and nearby neighborhoods were converted into multiple apartments over the past century. These buildings can be attractive investments, especially close to downtown employers, but they often carry complicated layouts, shared or added stairways, patchwork electrical and plumbing, and uncertain fire separation between units. Before renovating, we verify the legal unit count with the city, since adding or reconfiguring units may require zoning review. The scope then addresses fire separation, safe egress from every unit, electrical service sized for multiple households, heating systems that serve each unit appropriately and plumbing that can handle several kitchens and baths. Sherman Hill is a local historic district, so exterior changes such as window replacement, porch reconstruction and siding may require review, and we plan materials and schedules accordingly. Lead-safe practices apply throughout. When scoped carefully, these properties offer location and character that newer buildings cannot match, but they demand a realistic budget for hidden conditions.

sections.h2: Duplexes and fourplexes across the city
sections.body: On the north and south sides, Des Moines duplexes range from early twentieth century up-and-down houses to mid-century side-by-side buildings. Up-and-down duplexes typically share a basement and sometimes a heating system, and their rear stairways and porches often need repair to serve as a safe second exit. Side-by-side duplexes usually have separate utilities and mirrored layouts, which simplifies renovation. Fourplexes from the 1960s and 1970s have central stairways, shared laundry and units that have changed little since construction, along with possible asbestos in flooring or ceilings. Typical renovations include kitchens, baths, flooring and lighting in each unit, plus common-area updates, fire separation, upgraded smoke and carbon monoxide detection, and exterior work such as roofing and siding. Where heating or electrical service is shared, separating systems can improve net income, and we price that as its own line. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review separates unit costs from shared systems and common areas so you can compare the total with expected rents.

Many Des Moines small multifamily buildings are purchased with tenants in place, and preserving that income while improving the building is usually the goal. We typically renovate vacant units first, then schedule shared-system work such as roofing, heating replacements, electrical upgrades and basement waterproofing with advance notice and short, planned interruptions. Each occupied unit gets its interior renovation when it turns over. Heating work should be complete before winter, and any interruption to heat in cold weather must be brief and coordinated. Shared stairways, hallways and laundry rooms are cleaned and kept safe at the end of each workday, and lead-safe containment protects occupied units in older buildings. Because rental properties in Des Moines are subject to inspection, we sequence work so the building stays in good standing, and we build the inspection requirements into each unit's renovation. Your field manager coordinates access with tenants and your property manager and posts progress so you can follow every unit and the building as a whole.

faqs.q: Should I separate utilities in a Des Moines duplex?
faqs.a: It depends on the building and your hold period. Separating heat and electric shifts costs to tenants and can improve net income, but it requires new equipment, gas piping, venting and electrical work. Side-by-side duplexes often already have separate utilities, while older up-and-down duplexes may not. We price separation as a distinct line item so you can compare its cost with the expected benefit.

faqs.q: Can I add a unit to a Des Moines property?
faqs.a: That depends on zoning, the lot and the building. Adding a unit typically requires zoning review, building permits, fire separation, egress and utility work, and properties in historic districts may need additional review for exterior changes. We can evaluate the physical work and price it, while eligibility needs to be confirmed with the city before you commit to a purchase based on the extra unit.

faqs.q: How do you keep tenants safe during a building renovation?
faqs.a: We phase the work, contain dust with lead-safe practices in older buildings, keep shared areas clean and passable at the end of each day, and schedule utility interruptions with notice. Apartments with residents get their interior work only after the lease ends. Your field manager coordinates access with residents and your property manager throughout the project, adjusting the schedule when needed so nobody is left without heat, water or a safe way out.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Des Moines, IA | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor for Des Moines buyers, agents and lenders: bids, consultant coordination and draws for brick homes, ranches and duplexes.
fha-203k.intro: In Des Moines, the houses many first-time buyers can afford are the ones that need work: a north side foursquare with knob-and-tube wiring and an old boiler, a Beaverdale brick home with crumbling mortar and dated baths, or an east side ranch with a storm-damaged roof and a damp basement. The FHA 203(k) program lets those buyers finance the purchase and the renovation in a single mortgage, so the house can be brought up to standard right after closing. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, and we work with Des Moines buyers, real estate agents and loan officers to prepare bids, scopes and draw schedules that meet program requirements. Our role is to keep the renovation side organized so the closing stays on schedule and the buyer moves into a safe, updated home.

sections.h2: Choosing Limited or Standard in Des Moines
sections.body: Genstone works with the 203(k) thresholds stated on our site: the minimum repair amount is $5,000, a HUD consultant inspection applies above $15,000, and the Limited 203(k) caps repairs at $75,000 and excludes structural work. In Des Moines, a Limited 203(k) often fits a post-war ranch or Cape Cod that needs a new furnace, updated electrical, a roof replacement after storm damage, flooring and a kitchen refresh. A Standard 203(k) is the better choice for houses needing foundation repair, structural changes, major water management, extensive masonry rebuilding on a brick home or a full renovation of an older north side house. Choosing correctly at the beginning matters because switching programs midway can delay closing. Our estimators look for structural warning signs such as bowed basement walls, sagging framing, failing masonry and flood damage early, so the buyer and loan officer can pick the right program before underwriting begins in earnest.

sections.h2: Typical 203(k) work on Des Moines homes
sections.body: Des Moines 203(k) projects usually combine required health and safety repairs with improvements the buyer wants. Required items commonly include peeling paint on pre-1978 homes, which calls for lead-safe work, outdated or unsafe electrical, aging heating systems, roofs damaged by hail or wind, missing handrails and basement moisture. Masonry repairs on brick homes and asbestos in older flooring may also need attention. Optional improvements often focus on kitchens, baths, refinished floors and energy efficiency, such as attic insulation and new windows. Radon testing and mitigation are sensible additions in Iowa, particularly when the buyer plans to use the basement. If the property sits in a floodplain, the scope may need to account for additional requirements. We separate required and optional items in the bid so the buyer and lender can see what must be completed and what can be adjusted if the appraisal or budget is tight, which helps keep the loan on track and the closing on schedule.

sections.h2: From consultant write-up to final draw
sections.body: On a Standard 203(k), the HUD consultant prepares the work write-up, and our bid follows it line by line. We review the consultant's findings, identify items likely to cost more once walls or floors are opened in an older Des Moines home, and keep revisions to a minimum so the lender is not left waiting. After closing, our field manager pulls the permits the work requires from the Permit and Development Center, or the relevant suburb, and schedules inspections. The lender releases renovation funds in stages after each portion of work is inspected, and our field manager submits photos and notes with every draw request. If closing happens late in the year, exterior items such as roofing or masonry may be scheduled for spring, and we coordinate that timing with the lender. Buyers work with a single field manager who explains each step, while agents get a renovation process that stays organized from accepted offer to completion.

faqs.q: Can I use a 203(k) loan on a Des Moines duplex?
faqs.a: Yes. FHA allows 203(k) financing on one- to four-unit properties when the buyer lives in one of the units as a primary residence. That makes it a practical option for buyers considering Des Moines duplexes. Your loan officer confirms eligibility for the specific building, and we prepare a scope that covers each unit and the shared systems, such as the roof and heating.

faqs.q: How should a buyer start a 203(k) project with Genstone?
faqs.a: Send us the property address, listing details and, if available, the consultant's write-up or inspection report. An estimator walks the Des Moines house and writes the scope and bid in whatever format the buyer's lender uses. If the consultant has not visited yet, we can provide a preliminary estimate to help the buyer and agent decide whether the property is a good fit.

faqs.q: Is any money due to Genstone before 203(k) work begins?
faqs.a: No. After closing, renovation funds are held by the lender and released in stages once completed work is inspected, so there is no upfront payment to Genstone. Final payment follows completion and approval. Your field manager coordinates each draw inspection and provides the documentation the lender needs to release funds promptly. The buyer reviews progress and approves the finished work rather than paying contractors directly.

reo-renovation.title: REO Property Renovation in Des Moines, IA | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Des Moines REO and bank-owned renovations for servicers, banks, GSEs and investors: storm and water damage, mold, radon, code work and resale scopes.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Renovations in Des Moines
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned and vacant houses in Des Moines tend to deteriorate in predictable ways. Summer storms tear shingles and siding loose, and rain finds its way into attics and walls. Heavy downpours push water into basements, where it lingers and grows mold. In winter, a failed furnace can freeze and split supply lines, sending water through floors and ceilings. Add the usual vacancy issues of trespassing, theft of copper and code complaints, and a property can lose value quickly. Genstone Construction works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and investors buying REO in Des Moines and Polk County, and we are a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Together with Genstone Field Services, we can secure, inspect, document and repair vacant properties and prepare them for market.

sections.h2: Assessing storm, water and freeze damage
sections.body: Our first visit to a vacant Des Moines property is about understanding what has happened since it was last occupied. We look for roof and siding damage from hail or wind, check attics for active leaks, inspect basements for standing water, staining and mold, and pressure-test plumbing for freeze damage. Heating equipment is examined for cracked heat exchangers or boilers, and electrical systems are checked for water exposure or stolen wiring. Every condition is photographed and documented. Our scope separates urgent items, such as tarping damaged roofs, water extraction, mold remediation, winterization and securing doors and windows, from the repairs needed to prepare the house for sale. Asset managers can approve emergency work quickly while evaluating the remaining scope with full information. If the property is in or near a floodplain, we note any evidence of flood damage, which can affect both the repair plan and the resale strategy. The documentation supports insurance claims and investor reporting as well as repair decisions.

Vacant properties in Des Moines need regular attention to stay secure and compliant. Grass and weeds must be cut in summer, snow removed in winter, debris cleared and broken windows or doors secured. Neglected properties attract complaints and code enforcement, and outstanding orders can complicate a sale. Genstone Field Services provides property preservation, including lawn care, snow removal, debris removal, lock changes and periodic inspections, along with code compliance work. When the city has issued orders, we review them, price the repairs required to resolve them, pull permits through the Permit and Development Center and coordinate reinspection. If the property will be rented after sale, the city's rental inspection requirements also come into play, and we can scope the work so a buyer can register and lease the property without major corrections. Regular inspection reports with photos give asset managers a current view of each property, even when they are managing assets from another state.

Once a Des Moines REO is stabilized, the question becomes which repair level will produce the strongest sale. Many properties only need to reach a condition that FHA or conventional lenders will accept: working heat, safe electrical, sound plumbing, a functioning kitchen and bath, a roof without active leaks and a dry basement. That approach often suits north side and south side homes likely to sell to investors or first-time buyers. Other properties, such as a Beaverdale brick home or a well-located house near Drake or Waterbury, may justify a fuller renovation because owner-occupants will pay for move-in condition and character. Radon testing and mitigation can make a property more attractive to buyers who ask about it. We can price a stabilization scope, a lender-ready scope and a full renovation for the same property, allowing asset managers to compare cost with likely sale price. Permits, lien waivers, inspection results and milestone photos are compiled for the client, and one field manager stays accountable throughout.

faqs.q: Which REO clients does Genstone work with in Des Moines?
faqs.a: We work with mortgage servicers, banks with bank-owned inventory, REITs, investment funds and investors purchasing foreclosures, and Genstone is a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Each assignment includes an itemized scope, photo documentation and a single field manager for the life of the project, with Genstone Field Services available for preservation and compliance work while decisions about the asset are pending.

faqs.q: How do you address mold in a vacant Des Moines house?
faqs.a: We document and map affected areas, identify the moisture source, remove damaged materials and include remediation as a defined scope item. In Des Moines, mold often follows storm-related roof leaks, basement flooding during heavy rains or frozen pipes. Fixing the cause is part of the plan, so the problem does not return after the property is sold. Before-and-after photos are included in your records.

faqs.q: Should a Des Moines REO be tested for radon before sale?
faqs.a: It is often a good idea. Iowa has high radon levels, and many buyers, especially those using the basement as living space, ask about it. Testing and, where needed, installing a mitigation system is a modest cost that can remove an objection during the sale. We can include radon testing and mitigation as an optional line item in the scope.
